Nonlinear Latent Decoding for Inverse Scattering

An inverse network predicts coordinates that a nonlinear decoder turns into a reconstruction of the medium.

Anonymous submission · under blind review

Paper — forthcoming Code — forthcoming Abstract ↓

Reconstruction through latent coordinates

The measurement network predicts a compact vector instead of one value at every pixel. A nonlinear decoder maps that vector to the medium contrast. The decoder can learn from clean targets before inverse training, or it can be trained jointly with the inverse model.

Broad benchmark

One output change across five inverse operators

The pretrained frozen decoder is tested with five operator backbones, three target distributions, and three noise levels. It lowers mean relative NMSE by 34.4% and improves 44 of the 45 configurations.

At 12,800 paired Shapes examples, the nonlinear head improves all five backbones under the recorded training protocol. The reductions range from 9.4% for Transolver to 36.1% for OFormer, with wins in all 15 paired seed comparisons. Only the Transolver learning rate was retuned at this data size.

Scope of the evidence

The headline experiments use simulated scattering measurements. The official OrganAMNIST images are medical templates passed through the same simulated forward model. The paper also reports settings where spatial output performs better, including one measured-data comparison and a limited-angle linearized 3D experiment.

Abstract
Inverse scattering recovers the spatially varying contrast of a medium from measurements of its scattered wavefield. Most learned methods predict that contrast directly on a spatial grid. We instead have the inverse network predict coordinates that a nonlinear decoder maps to the reconstruction. Across five neural operator backbones, three synthetic target distributions, three noise levels, and multiple seeds, a pretrained frozen decoder lowers normalized mean squared error by 34.4% on average and improves 44 of 45 configurations. A scratch nonlinear synthesis head whose parameter count differs from the spatial head by 0.02% and whose compute differs by 0.07% lowers error by 46.2% with 200 Shapes pairs and 64.1% with 3,200, winning all ten paired seeds at each data size. The same matched scratch head improves MNIST, smooth fields, and organ-derived targets at 3,200 pairs. On the full official OrganAMNIST split, scratch and pretrained nonlinear heads lower error by 35.3% and 53.0%. With 12,800 paired Shapes examples, a capacity and compute matched pretrained head still improves all five backbones. Together, the experiments show that nonlinear coordinate prediction can be an effective reconstruction interface across the tested operator architectures under simulated scattering.
